Baseline algorithm for n weighted line segments. Test every pair for intersection in constant time, using the primitives already introduced. For an intersecting pair, the canonical-point paths to the intersection determine whether the two lifted edges stay within a sheet or switch sheets; this also takes constant time for line segments. Thus the lifted intersection graph is built in O(n²) time, with 2n vertices and O(n²) edges. Entering a lifted vertex v costs w(v). Run Dijkstra from c0 for each original segment c, read the distance to c1, and take the minimum, by the characterization theorem. The preceding binary-heap bound gives O(n³ log n), displayed as O-tilde(n³). The edge bound is worst-case; the reused four-segment example illustrates the construction and one search. A biclique is a complete bipartite subgraph; the host need not be bipartite. Here it contains triangle abc. Highlight K2,3, not merely a star. Extra edges within either vertex set are allowed because the biclique is not required to be induced.

Introduce the logic using a generic Problem X, not point separation. This is an example of a reduction one might prove, not a theorem about an unspecified problem. The reduction translates an O(n^(3-epsilon)) algorithm for X into an O(n^(3-epsilon-prime)) algorithm for APSP. The two positive constants need not agree: for each fixed epsilon>0, the reduction provides some epsilon-prime>0. Here n refers to the input size of the respective problem, with the reduction accounting for any size change. On the next build, take the contrapositive underneath the original implication. Combining it with the APSP hypothesis rules out such an algorithm for X. Only after this generic explanation do we introduce minimum-weight triangle and then the geometric reduction.
The two triangles weigh 7 and 12. Highlight the smaller one, including its vertices and weight labels; fade everything else. Williams & Williams show that APSP and minimum-weight triangle are equivalent under truly subcubic reductions: a fixed improvement over cubic time for either gives a fixed improvement for the other. The epsilons need not match. A common shift of edge weights makes triangle weights nonnegative without changing the optimum.

The talk establishes the weighted line-segment upper bound and the APSP-based conditional lower bound. The final mention of the stronger bound is included at the user’s request; no other lower-bound proof is presented. The near-quadratic bound uses a different hypothesis, whose details are outside this talk.
